title: Chapter 28
paragraphs: The morning after the ball, early, Anna Arkadyevna sent her husband a telegram that she was leaving Moscow the same day.

"No, I have to go, I have to go," she explained to her sister-in-law about the change in her plans, in a tone that suggested she had so many things to remember there was no enumerating them: "no, it had really better be today!"
Stepan Arkadyevitch was not dining at home, but he promised to come and see his sister off at seven o'clock.

Kitty did not come either, sending a note that she had a headache. Dolly and Anna dined alone with the children and the English governess. Whether it was that the children were fickle, or that they had keen senses and felt that Anna was quite different that day from what she had been when they had taken such a fancy to her, that she was no longer interested in them — but they had abruptly dropped their play with their aunt, and their love for her, and were quite indifferent that she was leaving. Anna spent the whole morning absorbed in preparations for her departure. She wrote notes to her Moscow acquaintances, did her accounts, and packed. To Dolly it seemed Anna was not in a placid state of mind, but in that worried mood Dolly knew well in herself, the kind that does not come without cause and usually covers dissatisfaction with self. After dinner Anna went up to her room to dress, and Dolly followed her.
"How strange you are today," Dolly said to her.

"I? Do you think so? I'm not strange, but I'm in a nasty mood. I'm like this sometimes. I keep feeling as if I could cry. It's very stupid, but it'll pass," Anna said quickly, and bent her flushed face over a tiny bag in which she was packing a nightcap and some cambric handkerchiefs. Her eyes were unusually bright, and continually filled with tears. "In the same way I didn't want to leave Petersburg, and now I don't want to leave here."
"You came here and did a good deed," said Dolly, looking at her intently.
Anna looked at her with eyes wet with tears.

"Don't say that, Dolly. I've done nothing, and I could do nothing. I often wonder why people are all in league to spoil me. What have I done, and what could I have done? In your heart there was love enough to forgive..."
"If it hadn't been for you, God knows what would have happened! How fortunate you are, Anna," said Dolly. "Everything is clear and good in your heart."
"Every heart has its own _skeletons_, as the English say."
"You don't have any sort of _skeleton_, do you? Everything is so clear in you."
"I do!" said Anna suddenly, and, unexpectedly after her tears, a sly, ironical smile curved her lips.
"Well, then, he's amusing, your _skeleton_, at any rate, and not depressing," said Dolly, smiling.

"No, he's depressing. Do you know why I'm going today instead of tomorrow? It's a confession that's weighing on me, and I want to make it to you," said Anna, letting herself drop firmly into an armchair and looking straight into Dolly's face.
And to her surprise Dolly saw that Anna was blushing up to her ears, up to the curly black ringlets on her neck.

"Yes," Anna went on. "Do you know why Kitty didn't come to dinner? She's jealous of me. I've spoiled... I've been the cause of that ball being a torture to her instead of a pleasure. But truly, truly, it's not my fault, or only my fault a little bit," she said, daintily drawling the words "a little bit."
"Oh, how like Stiva you said that!" Dolly said, laughing.
Anna was hurt.
"Oh, no, oh no! I am not Stiva," she said, frowning. "That's why I'm telling you — because I could never let myself doubt myself for an instant," said Anna.

But at the very moment she was saying the words, she felt they were not true. She was not merely doubting herself; she felt emotion at the thought of Vronsky, and was leaving earlier than she had planned simply to avoid meeting him.
"Yes, Stiva told me you danced the mazurka with him, and that he..."
"You can't imagine how absurdly the whole thing came about. I only meant to do a bit of matchmaking, and instead it turned out quite differently. Possibly against my own will..."
She crimsoned and stopped.
"Oh, they feel it right away?" said Dolly.
"But I'd be in despair if there were anything serious in it on his side," Anna cut in. "And I'm certain it will all be forgotten, and Kitty will stop hating me."

"All the same, Anna, I'll tell you the truth — I'm not very keen on this marriage for Kitty. And it's better for it to come to nothing, if he, Vronsky, is capable of falling in love with you in a single day."

"Oh, heavens, that would be too silly!" said Anna, and once again a deep flush of pleasure spread over her face as she heard the idea that was absorbing her put into words. "And so here I am going off, having made an enemy of Kitty, whom I liked so much! Ah, how sweet she is! But you'll set it right, Dolly? Won't you?"
Dolly could hardly suppress a smile. She loved Anna, but she enjoyed seeing that even she had her weaknesses.
"An enemy? That can't be."
"I did so want all of you to care for me, the way I care for you, and now I care for you more than ever," said Anna, her eyes filling with tears. "Ah, how silly I am today!"
She passed her handkerchief over her face and began dressing.
At the very moment of starting, Stepan Arkadyevitch arrived — late, rosy and good-humored, smelling of wine and cigars.

Anna's emotionalism infected Dolly, and when she embraced her sister-in-law for the last time, she whispered, "Remember, Anna, what you've done for me — I shall never forget. And remember that I love you, and shall always love you as my dearest friend!"
"I don't know why," said Anna, kissing her and hiding her tears.
"You understood me, and you understand. Good-bye, my darling!"
